title: Capitals and final sigma

objectives.can: Match capital letters to their lower-case forms and read σ and ς as one letter.

explanation.summary: Greek has capital letters, and its sigma has a second shape, ς, which is used only at the end of a word. Neither is a new letter. You meet both at once in the first verse of Matthew, where the names are capitalised and most words end in ς.

sections.heading: Capitals and lower case
body: Each letter has a capital form (Α, Β, Γ …) and a lower-case form (α, β, γ …). They have the same name and the same sound. The first table of this lesson pairs them. Some capitals look just like the lower case enlarged (Κ κ, Ο ο, Ζ ζ); others are different shapes (Γ γ, Δ δ, Λ λ, Σ σ, Ω ω) and must simply be learned.

The earliest copies of the New Testament were written in capitals alone, with no gaps between words. Lower-case letters, word-spacing and capitals as we use them in printed Greek are conventions of later copyists and modern editors.

sections.heading: Where an edition uses capitals
body: In the edition used in this library, capitals mark personal names and places (Ἀβραάμ, Ἰσαάκ, Δαυίδ, Ἰωάννης), the first word of a paragraph (as in Ἐγένετο, which opens John 1:6), and the first word of a sentence of direct speech (as in Τίς, which opens the question in John 1:22). Within a sentence, every other word is lower case.

Other editions follow other habits. Matthew 1:1 prints χριστοῦ with a small letter, and John 1:17 prints Χριστοῦ with a capital. The choice is the editor's, so a capital letter is a useful hint that a word is a name, never a proof.

sections.heading: Two shapes of sigma
body: The letter sigma is written σ at the beginning or in the middle of a word and ς at the end. It is one letter with one sound and one name. In σκοτία the sigma is first, so it is σ. In Ἰσαάκ it is in the middle, so it is σ. In λόγος it is last, so it is ς. A word such as γενέσεως has both, one in the middle and one at the end.
The capital has only one shape, Σ. It stands at the start of a name, as in Σίμων.
The final shape is a matter of spelling: no word ever ends in σ, and no word has ς anywhere but at its end.

sections.heading: A mark before a capital
body: Names such as Ἀβραάμ and Ἰσαάκ begin with a vowel, so they carry a small mark in front of the capital. These marks are breathings, taught in G0.2.2. For now treat them as part of the letter and read the capital beneath them.

misunderstandings: A capital is not a different letter. Α and α are one letter, alpha, in two sizes.
ς is not a seventh vowel or a new consonant. It is sigma at the end of a word, and it sounds the same as σ.
Do not write ς at the start or in the middle of a word, and do not write σ at the end.
A capital letter does not prove that a word is a name. Editions differ, and this edition also capitalises the first word of a paragraph or of a spoken sentence.

deeper.heading: Why the final sigma exists
body: The earliest manuscripts of the New Testament were written in capital letters, and in them sigma had no final form. The rule that ς stands at the end of a word belongs to later handwriting and to the printed editions you read now. It carries no difference of sound or of word.

examples.analysis: Ἰησοῦ, Δαυίδ and Ἀβραάμ are names, and each begins with a capital: iota, delta and alpha. Βίβλος, the first word of the book, also has a capital. Notice that Ἰησοῦ has a sigma in the middle, so it is σ; this form of the name ends in a vowel and has no final sigma.

examples.analysis: Three capitalised names and a word that ends in ς. Ἀβραάμ, Ἰσαάκ and Ἰούδαν are names; Ἰσαάκ has a sigma in the middle, so it is σ. ἀδελφοὺς ('brothers') ends in ς, because its last letter is a sigma.

reading.why: The opening of Matthew is a list of capitalised names (Ἀβραάμ, Ἰσαάκ, Ἰακώβ, Δαυίδ) and of words ending in ς, so every capital and every final sigma of the lesson is in front of you. Read for the letters, not the meaning.
